result:
I would erase the human capacity for self-deception regarding the suffering of others.

Most of the world’s profound cruelty, destruction, and systemic injustice doesn't stem from pure, cartoonish malice. It stems from distance and abstraction. It happens because people are extraordinarily good at convincing themselves that the harm they cause—or profit from—isn't real, isn't that bad, or is happening to people who somehow deserve it or don't feel it the same way.

If that illusion were fundamentally broken—if a person could not make a choice without vividly, instinctively experiencing the exact weight of its consequences on the people it impacts—the incentives of the world would transform overnight. 

A politician signing a war declaration would have to feel the sudden, blinding terror of the civilians beneath the bombs. A corporate executive deciding to dump toxic waste or strip a community of its livelihood would feel the slow sickness and desperation of the families living downstream. 

It wouldn't take away free will, nor would it force everyone to agree on how to solve problems. But it would destroy the buffer of indifference. You wouldn't need to persuade people to care about the climate, poverty, or violence; the impossibility of ignoring the pain would make the status quo unendurable. Violence and exploitation would cease not out of moral perfection, but because hurting someone else would feel indistinguishable from hurting oneself.
